items.stem: What distinguishes an argument from a mere assertion?

options.text: An argument offers reasons or evidence to support its conclusion
options.rationale: Correct: an argument supplies support; an assertion simply states a claim.

options.text: An argument is always longer than an assertion
options.rationale: Length does not define an argument.
An assertion may be true or false; it just lacks stated support.

options.text: An argument must be spoken rather than written
options.rationale: Medium is irrelevant to whether something is an argument.

items.explanation: Correct: an argument supplies support; an assertion simply states a claim.
items.provenance: original Mastemy item drafted by an AI agent; no external question source

items.stem: Which TWO are sound reasons to doubt that a correlation proves causation?

options.text: A third factor may cause both variables to move together
options.rationale: Correct: a confounding variable can produce correlation without direct causation.

options.text: The direction of causation may be reversed from what is assumed
options.rationale: Correct: the effect may actually be driving the supposed cause.

options.text: Correlation always proves causation when the data set is large
options.rationale: Sample size does not turn correlation into causation.

options.text: Any two numbers that rise together must be causally linked
options.rationale: Co-movement alone does not establish a causal link.

options.text: Causation is impossible to ever establish
options.rationale: Causation can be established with appropriate evidence, such as controlled study.

items.explanation: Correct: a confounding variable can produce correlation without direct causation.

options.text: Favouring information that supports what you already believe and discounting the rest
options.rationale: Correct: confirmation bias skews attention toward belief-confirming evidence.

options.text: Confirming every fact with a second source
options.rationale: That describes verification, not a bias.

options.text: A fallacy that only affects statistics
options.rationale: It is a cognitive bias, not limited to statistics.

options.text: The tendency to change your mind too easily
options.rationale: Confirmation bias is resistance to disconfirming evidence, not fickleness.

items.explanation: Correct: confirmation bias skews attention toward belief-confirming evidence.
